title: Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Bill
what_it_is: Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Bill

sections.label: Select Committee on falsehoods
sections.summary: Parliament appointed a Select Committee that received 169 written representations and produced a 279-page report on four broad issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On 5 January, we asked Parliament and Parliament did so appoint a Select Committee (SC) to examine four broad issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It received 169 written representations from a broad cross-section of society.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The SC then prepared a detailed 279-page report – many of the issues which have been raised since the Bill was first tabled in Parliament, repeat the points that were canvassed quite extensively during the SC hearings; points like falsehoods and how to define them and differentiate them from opinions; the possible different decision-making models like executive powers, independent body, Courts; and other such points.

sections.label: MDA news website licensing scheme
sections.summary: In 2013 the MDA introduced individual licensing for news websites reporting regularly on Singapore, requiring removal of breaching content within 24 hours and a $50,000 performance bond.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2013, the then-Media Development Authority (MDA) put in place a new individual licensing scheme for news websites which report regularly on Singapore; and also required online news sites to remove within 24 hours content which was in breach of standards and post a performance bond of $50,000.

sections.label: Class Licensing Scheme takedowns
sections.summary: From 1996 to 2019, takedowns under the Class Licensing Scheme were used mostly for pornographic, sex solicitation, sex chat, religiously-offensive and extremist content.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Post 2013, discussions online carried on as before.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, from 1996 to 2019, after 23 years that you have had the Class Licensing Scheme, takedowns were used mostly for sites and services with pornographic content, solicitation of sex, sex chats, religiously-offensive content, extremist content.

sections.label: Four commented aspects of Bill
sections.summary: Opponents commented on four aspects of the Bill: takedown of material, takedown ordered by Ministers, definition of public interest, and definition of falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The four aspects of the Bill that have been commented upon by those who are opposed are: (a) takedown of material; (b) takedown can be ordered by Ministers; (c) definition of public interest; and (d) definition of falsehoods.

sections.label: Telecoms Act section 45 repeal
sections.summary: Section 45 of the Telecoms Act was repealed yesterday and subsumed under the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act and the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Section 45 of the Telecoms Act was repealed yesterday, subsumed under the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act (MOA) and the Penal Code.

sections.label: POFMA falsehood determination appeals
sections.summary: Under POFMA, on the determination of falsehoods, Court oversight is by way of direct appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: According to the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), the Bill, on the determination of falsehoods, the Court oversight is by way of direct appeal.

sections.label: New narrower online falsehoods legislation
sections.summary: After the SC process, they decided on new legislation with narrower powers focused on online falsehoods, with calibrated remedies and greater judicial oversight.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: After the SC process, we decided, let us have new legislation with a narrower set of powers than under existing legislation, focused on online falsehoods, with remedies that are more calibrated and provide for greater judicial oversight over executive action, designed specifically for the Internet rather than rely on existing legislation, and to deal specifically with online falsehoods, rather than the broader areas that are covered under the BA.

sections.label: Territoriality provision for Internet intermediaries
sections.summary: The only point requiring statutory amendment under the BA was the territoriality provision to include Internet intermediaries based outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The only thing, and the only thing that would have required a statutory amendment would have been one point under the BA, that is, to the territoriality provision to include Internet intermediaries based outside of Singapore.

sections.label: Bill targets fast online falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill was fashioned to deal specifically with falsehoods spread online with speed, proportionality, and greater powers for the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill, on the other hand, was fashioned to deal specifically with falsehoods that can be spread online with incredible speed, in a targeted manner, and to address such falsehoods with speed, with proportionality, and with the Courts given greater powers.

sections.label: Bill restricts Government powers on falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill addresses serious risks while cutting down existing powers, restricting the Government's powers and giving judges greater oversight.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill is an attempt to deal with some of these very real, serious risks which all societies face.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But at the same time, in a carefully considered manner, with the Government deciding that we should come before the House and put forward something that, in a way, cuts down on the existing powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And put forward a new Bill that actually restricts the Government's powers compared with today, but focused on online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And voluntarily, compared with existing legislation, say, if the House agrees, let us give greater oversight to the judges, and let us make it much faster.

sections.summary: Populism reigns in some Latin American countries and has gained footholds in Asia, and the Eurasia Group assesses it is likely to intensify and spread over the coming decade.

The result will be a set of unyielding, centrifugal forces, creating a global environment described by the Eurasia Group as "the most dangerous it has been in decades".

sections.label: Bill on new media falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill attempts to deal with one part of the problem: serious problems arising from falsehoods spread through new media.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill is an attempt to deal with one part of the problem: the serious problems arising from falsehoods spread through new media.

sections.label: Sources of social media attacks
sections.summary: Attacks using falsehoods on social media come from foreign countries, profit-driven actors, deliberate actors for political ends, and people with prejudices seeking to harm other groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The attack using falsehoods on social media comes from several sources: (a) foreign countries using information warfare; (b) profit-driven actors; (c) deliberate actors, for political ends; and (d) people with prejudices, seeking to harm other groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: General Gerasimov, Russia’s military Chief of Staff, there is a doctrine named after him called the Gerasimov Doctrine.

sections.label: Shashi Jayakumar on information warfare
sections.summary: Dr Shashi Jayakumar said seeding internal opposition is important in modern information warfare and that a technological tsunami lets aggressor states subvert individual slices of a target country.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Dr Shashi Jayakumar said that in modern information warfare, "seeding internal opposition within the target country is extremely important." And he said that "technological tsunami" has given aggressor states the ability to "subvert individual slices" of the target country in a manner unthinkable just two to three decades ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In his words: "It is easier for the adversary to achieve its objectives if the society of the state being attacked believes that their country is a failed state that does not care for the interests and needs of the population, and the loss of current statehood will bring better living conditions." Singapore is a specific and vulnerable target for some very precise reasons.

sections.label: French falsehoods and Yellow Vest misinformation

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A false tweet that the White House had been bombed led to a massive fall in the stock market.

I will mention three tools: fake accounts; digital advertising; and algorithms used by platforms to rank content.

sections.summary: Legislation is essential and must work with non-legislative measures, and the Bill's powers have to be used when there is public interest and falsehood.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But you need legislation at the same time and you have got to have legislation work with non-legislative measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But in the kind of situations we are talking about, there is no question whatsoever that legislation is essential and this Bill is about legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Separately, the Government has committed to a whole series of non-legislative matters; and Parliament can question the different Ministries ranging from education to public education to media literacy, there is a variety of things.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But when there is public interest involved and there is falsehood, and the Nominated Members accept the Bill is necessary, then there can be no argument and the Bill has to be used and the powers under the Act have got to be used.

sections.label: Proportionality in the Bill
sections.summary: Proportionality is incorporated into the Bill's requirements as a legal test, allowing the power only when necessary or expedient in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Proportionality is already incorporated into the requirements of under the Bill and it is stronger than your proposal because when it is incorporated in the Bill, it is part of the legal requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the legal test already requires that the power can only be exercised when it is necessary or expedient in the public interest to do so.

sections.label: Council functions under current structure
sections.summary: The passage states that all functions of this council can be achieved under the current structure of the Executive and Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All of the functions of this council can be achieved under the current structure of the Executive and Parliament.

sections.label: Relying on current institutions
sections.summary: The passage argues it is more effective to rely on current institutions like Parliament and the Courts for direct accountability.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You do not keep creating bodies and then who checks on them?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it is really more effective to rely on the strength of our current institutions – direct accountability.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, you have Parliament, you have the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Anytime there is a question, it can be challenged in Courts, it can be challenged in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you keep getting it wrong, the electorate will have something to say about it.

sections.label: SC findings and action areas
sections.summary: The passage lists the SC's key findings on online falsehoods and its five broad areas for action.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: A few of its key findings include: first, that there are increasing signs of the phenomenon in Singapore and evidence of foreign disinformation; two, there is a real risk of slow-drip falsehoods exploiting Singapore diversity to damage society in the long term; thirdly, Singapore is also vulnerable due to its regional circumstances.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The SC gave five broad areas for action: first, nurture an informed public; second, reinforce social cohesion and trust; third, promote fact-checking; fourth, disrupt online falsehoods; and fifth, deal with threats to national security and sovereignty.

sections.label: Committee accepted legal analysis
sections.summary: The passage states the Committee accepted legal analysis that existing laws were inadequate and concluded new laws are needed.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Essentially, the Committee accepted robust and credible legal analysis showing that existing laws in Singapore were inadequate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: It concluded that new laws are needed and, importantly, the SC found that the concerns over free speech could be addressed using a calibrated approach in legislation.

sections.label: SC recommendation on government powers
sections.summary: The passage states the SC unanimously recommended that the Government should have powers to swiftly disrupt online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The unanimous recommendation of the SC was that the Government should have powers to swiftly disrupt online falsehoods.

sections.label: Oversight of Internet intermediaries
sections.summary: The passage states it provides regulatory oversight of Internet intermediaries, implementing recommendations 17 to 20 of the SC's report.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: It provides regulatory oversight of Internet intermediaries to ensure that they take effective measures to prevent and combat the problems.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This implements recommendations 17 to 20 of the SC’s report.

sections.label: Codes of Practice for platforms
sections.summary: The Bill allows for the issuing of Codes of Practice that bind the platforms.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Bill also allows for the issuing of Codes of Practice binding the platforms.

sections.label: Minister Directions and Courts
sections.summary: The Minister will be empowered to issue Directions against falsehoods in the public interest, with the Courts having the final say on falsity.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Minister will be empowered to issue Directions against falsehoods, where it is in the public interest to do so.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Courts will have the final say over what is false.

sections.label: Disabling access to falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill provides for disabling access to falsehoods, where it is in the public interest to do so.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Besides corrections powers, the Bill also provides for disabling of access to falsehoods, where it is in the public interest to do so.

sections.label: Conditions for issuing Directions
sections.summary: Two conditions must be satisfied before Directions can be issued: a false statement of fact communicated in Singapore, and public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Two conditions must be satisfied before the Directions can be issued.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: First, a false statement of fact must be communicated in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Second, it is in the public interest to issue a Direction.

sections.label: Directions against Internet statements
sections.summary: Directions can also be issued against false statements communicated over the Internet, regardless of the platform.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Directions can also be issued against false "statements" communicated over the Internet, regardless of the platform.

sections.label: False video mobilising disruption
sections.summary: A false video of Muslims celebrating a terrorist attack generated 500,000 views and mobilised thousands to disrupt a real event.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: We saw earlier the false video of Muslims celebrating a terrorist attack.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: That video generated 500,000 views within hours of being posted on one Facebook page.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: There was a real event that actually took place, but it was not a pro-communist rally.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: It took less than 24 hours for the falsehood to mobilise thousands to turn up at the event to disrupt it and to protest.

sections.label: Hoax spread and Bill remedies
sections.summary: A hoax spread fast and wiped out $4 billion, so the Bill's remedies aim to counter quick, wide, deep falsehood spread, based on the SC Report.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Within four hours, there were 47,000 tweets and the topic had hit Twitter’s "trending" list of most popular topics within hours.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The hoax wiped out $4 billion in market value within five hours.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: So, the essence of the remedies is that they have to be able to address and counter the quick, wide and deep spread of falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The provision in this Bill is based closely on the recommendations in the SC Report and the Bill seeks to achieve these outcomes.

sections.label: Protection from Falsehoods Online Bill
sections.summary: The Government has proposed the Protection from Falsehoods Online and Manipulation Bill, referred to as POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government has proposed the Protection from Falsehoods Online and Manipulation Bill before the House today, what I will henceforth refer to as POFMA.

sections.label: Workers' Party opposes POFMA
sections.summary: The Workers' Party opposes the Bill, objecting that the Executive should not be the initial decision-maker on false statements of fact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In comments to The Straits Times last Saturday about whether the Bill could have the unintended effect of self-censorship, the Minister said, "We need to educate the public that the Bill applies only to people putting out falsehoods and that various Ministries like the Education Ministry is working on public education in this area." Mr Speaker, the Workers' Party opposes this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: All the Workers’ Party Members will speak against it and our objections centre primarily around a fundamental matter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, we do not agree that the Executive should be the initial decision-maker on matters surrounding false statements of fact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While the Government must legitimately be able to apply to shut down malicious actors, a Court order should legitimise this action that needs to be undertaken.

sections.label: Report considered three options
sections.summary: The Report considered the Courts, an independent body or ombudsman issuing directions, and social media companies acting on user notifications with recourse to Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First was the Courts; the second was the establishment of an independent body or ombudsman that would issue directions; and third, the Report considered the prospects of social media companies themselves acting upon notification of falsehoods by users with a recourse to the Courts.

sections.label: Clause 2(2) deems misleading false
sections.summary: Clause 2(2) legislates that a statement can be deemed false by the Government if it is misleading, wholly or in part.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In fact, clause 2(2) legislates that a statement can be deemed by the Government to be false if it is misleading – whether wholly or in part, and whether on its own or in the context in which it appears.

sections.label: Clause 10 Minister directions
sections.summary: Clause 10 legislates that any Minister can issue a whole range of directions if the Minister thinks it is in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In addition to clause 2, clause 10 legislates that any Minister can issue a whole range of directions if that Minister is of the opinion that it would be in the public interest to issue it.

sections.label: POFMA public interest definition
sections.summary: The passage states clause 4 gives a non-exhaustive definition of 'in the public interest', which is part of the condition for directions under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Such a conclusion would explain why even moderate Singaporeans have raised concerns about the prospect of POFMA having a chilling effect on the public discourse at the hands of a very easily triggered Executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Now, if an exceedingly low threshold to trigger Part 3 was not enough, the explanatory statement of the Bill at page 69 clarifies that the six scenarios of what would qualify as the public interest are actually only the tip of the iceberg.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I quote the explanatory statement: "Clause 4 gives a non-exhaustive" and let me stress this again "a non-exhaustive definition of the expression ‘in the public interest’, which is part of the condition for making the various directions under this Bill." So, in fact, what this Bill is really saying is that clause 4 is merely a precursor to another potentially unknown list of definitions of what could be in the public interest.

sections.label: POFMA appeal grounds to Courts
sections.summary: POFMA limits appeal grounds to the Courts to three circumstances in clause 17, and Judicial Review covers only legality, not merits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Instead, POFMA limits the grounds for appeal to the Courts to three circumstances as listed in clause 17.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While Judicial Review nonetheless applies, it is a high bar as Judicial Review does not cover the merits of the Minister's decision, but only its legality.

sections.label: POHA remedies and Harassment Courts
sections.summary: New POHA sections 15 and 16 provide identical remedies for companies and individuals, with Harassment Courts handling all online falsehood applications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The new sections 15 and 16 of POHA envisage identical remedies, such as stop publication and correction orders that can be invoked by companies and individuals in Singapore, in addition to orders sought against tech companies upon application to the Harassment Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Harassment Courts, dealing with all online falsehood applications, from individuals and companies and the Government, would also result in a consistent application of the law in matters involving online falsehoods and misleading information, resulting in not only greater clarity for all parties but would help in public education on permissible and impermissible forms of expression.

sections.label: Courts handling viral falsehoods
sections.summary: The passage recalls Edwin Tong's clarification that Courts can try to deal with an online falsehood threatening to go viral in four to five hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Here, I think it is helpful for me to come back to the clarification from Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong that in the case of an online falsehood that threatens to go viral in four to five hours, if I heard the Senior Minister of State correctly, the answer was, the Courts can try to deal with that situation.

sections.label: Bill regulating free speech expression
sections.summary: The passage states the Bill would regulate what some reasonable people may interpret as free speech under Article 14, questioning whether Courts are better placed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The fact that the Bill would have to regulate what some reasonable people may well interpret as an expression of free speech under Article 14 of our Constitution, must give us reason to pause and question whether the Courts are better placed to exercise judgement on this point.

sections.label: Political misleading statements against candidates
sections.summary: The passage states some misleading statements will be completely political, aimed at lowering the esteem and political prospects of election candidates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Some misleading statements will be completely political in nature, aimed at lowering the esteem and political prospects of election candidates.

sections.label: Decision-maker conflict perception
sections.summary: The decision-maker must be perceived as free of conflict when deciding on online falsehoods and manipulation as defined by the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Suspicious will be raised and perceptions could be formed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But it is precisely because of these very reasons that the decision-maker must be perceived to be free of conflict in deciding on matters concerning online falsehoods and manipulation as defined by the Bill.

sections.label: Courts trying such cases
sections.summary: The speaker says that while Courts can try, it would be very difficult for a Court to marshal details and facts and decide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Would Mr Pritam Singh accept that, while I said that the Courts can try, I went on to say that it would be very difficult and I went on to explain also that in the context of this kind of cases, it would be extremely difficult for a Court to have a proper marshaling of the details and the facts and to decide on the case.

sections.label: Courts and expedited procedure
sections.summary: The speaker believes Courts can act speedily under an expedited procedure, but says it is not possible within five to six hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The point I think that needs to be made here with regard to the use of the Courts is that, with an expedited procedure – which the Senior Minister of State also confirmed under POHA, simple claims form – there is room, in my belief, that the Courts can still represent a decision-making authority which can act speedily.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The point that Mr Pritam Singh is trying to put across is that the Courts can do so in a matter of – and, I think, to say, in the Member's words – five to six hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And I have explained earlier that whilst the Courts can try, it will be very difficult to do so, especially having regard to the fact that they will have to access the merits of the matter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And it is not possible to bring the case within that period of time.

sections.label: Speed of online falsehoods
sections.summary: The speed of online falsehoods cannot be addressed effectively by the usual judicial process and requires timely executive action.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The speed with which online falsehoods spread and threaten public interest cannot be addressed effectively using the usual judicial process and require timely executive action.

sections.label: Bill scope versus German French laws
sections.summary: The Bill applies to any person or organisation deemed to be spreading fake news, unlike German and French legislation limited to tele-media service providers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This allows for contents with correction notice to be still available for debates and, therefore, more informed decision-making and this is, indeed, progressive.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, one feature to note in our current Bill is that it applies to any person or organisation deemed to be spreading fake news.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The aforementioned German and French legislation limit the scope of the law to only tele-media service providers operating Internet platforms.

sections.label: Broad definition of terms
sections.summary: The definition of statement of fact, public interest and diminution of public confidence is very broad.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The definition of what constitutes "statement of fact, public interest and diminution of public confidence" is very broad.

sections.label: Fake news bill oversight concerns
sections.summary: The speaker raises the dilemma of who watches the watchers, urges an expeditious appeal process in the primary legislation, and notes the lack of an independent oversight council.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is the characteristic dilemma of "Who watches the watchers?" In a democratic society, the rule of law should apply to everyone.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I acknowledge Minister Shanmugan's assurance that members of the public have the recourse of appealing the Government's decision via the Court and he has also advised that the process will be relatively "fast and inexpensive".

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Bill does not specify the prompt access to recourse in the event of a wrongly executed takedown of supposed fake news.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Although I understand a timeline for appeal will be stated in the subsidiary legislation, I strongly urge the need for an expeditious appeal process to be included in the primary legislation, for example, not more than how many days.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The next point of contention is the lack of an independent oversight council for checks and balances.

sections.label: Party Whip and free speech
sections.summary: The speaker appeals to lift the Party Whip for tomorrow's vote, citing 170 written representations and protests from civil groups over the Bill's impact on free speech.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Government will imperil itself if the people perceive that this Bill takes too much liberty with their freedom of speech.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I appeal to the House to seriously consider lifting the Party Whip and allow Members to vote according to their conscience for tomorrow's voting.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Many civil groups harbour genuine concerns over this Bill, as evident by the 170 written representations from individuals and organisations who submitted to the SC, and this includes numerous open letters and joint statements published in protest of this Bill from both local and international fronts.

sections.label: Czech propaganda survey
sections.summary: A Czech survey showed 53% of Czechs believed both pro-Russian and anti-Russian propaganda existed in Czech public space and could not trust anything.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the Czech Republic, a survey showed that 53% of Czechs believed that there was both pro-Russian and anti-Russian propaganda in the Czech public space, and they could not trust anything.

sections.label: Banksy fake news shares
sections.summary: A fake news story about Banksy's arrest received 60,402 shares, while nine debunking articles by major outlets took to reach the same total.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In October 2014, NationalReport.net, a fake news website, published a story that street artist Banksy had been arrested in London and that the City of London Police had identified Banksy as Paul William Horner, a 36-year-old male born in Liverpool, England.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This article received a total of 60,402 shares on Twitter and Facebook.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: By contrast, it took nine debunking articles by major news outlets, such as The Independent, The Huffington Post, and so on, to reach the same total of 60,000 shares.

sections.label: SC report breaking virality
sections.summary: The SC report's recommendation 12 states the measures must break virality by being effective in a matter of hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the words of the SC report, recommendation 12, "The measures will need to achieve the objective of breaking virality by being effective in a matter of hours." Hours!

sections.label: Statutory appeal and judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker identifies a statutory appeal mechanism and judicial review, and says the debate should not get tongue-tied over philosophy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The first is a statutory appeal mechanism, and the second is judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: I do not think we should be debating on philosophy and getting tongue-tied over illusions of philosophy.

sections.label: Support for Executive first-instance decision
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill, citing risks of falsehoods to a multiracial society and an accelerated court review process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: I do not think that we should be blind to the fact that there are major issues around the world and that falsehoods can tear a multiracial and multi-religious society like Singapore, can tear it quite quickly and quite swiftly, and we must guard against that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Therefore, for principle reasons and for practical reasons, I am in support of the model of allowing the Executive to make the first instance decision, and then have it reviewed by the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And we have heard the Minister state that in subsidiary legislation this is going to be an accelerated process – actually within nine days, you could get a hearing if, indeed, the complainant uses his right quickly within the 14 days that he has.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: So, for these reasons, I do not think we should be waving a banner of freedom of speech without understanding the consequences of what that entails in dynamic situations where falsehoods can catch like fire in hay.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And for those reasons, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Falsehoods undermine trust in institutions
sections.summary: The passage states that falsehoods undermining trust in public institutions can impede policymaking and crisis response.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Para 24, page 5, "Falsehoods that undermine trust in public institutions can impede constructive policymaking and the ability to respond to crisis and threats effectively.

sections.label: Stemming online falsehoods swiftly
sections.summary: The passage cites report paragraphs and a recommendation on providing swift access to facts and discrediting falsehoods swiftly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: The importance of stemming the spread of online falsehoods – para 357(a). "Specific objectives – Provide swift access to the facts" – para 361 of the report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: And in page 103 of the report, Part c: "neutralise false amplifiers,...swiftly." I think this brings to bear why in recommendation No 12 at page 133, we want to be able to discredit falsehoods swiftly.

sections.label: Council functions and adjudication role
sections.summary: The speaker reads council functions in the Order Paper Supplement and says the Executive plus Judiciary oversight is best.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: I studied the Order Paper Supplement and, actually, under the functions of the council under (h) at page 7, it says "to perform such functions as the Minister may, by order publish...assign, provided such functions do not compromise the independence of the Panel." It would seem to me that this council suggested through this suggested amendment envisions practising some of the Ministerial functions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: And in addition to that, at (f) at page 7, under functions of the Council, it says "to liaise with scientific, specialist and technical experts to advise the Government on examining contested facts of a specialist nature." And it seems that the Council that this amendment envisions is taking on the adjudication role of what is fact and what is not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: So, I do think that we should take it seriously, the amendment, look at it for what it is and, in my considered view, the Executive plus an oversight of the Judiciary is the best way forward.

sentences.speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
sentences.text: We are not suggesting that the oversight committee take over this Executive decision, so we still maintain for Ministers to make the Executive decision.

sections.label: Workers' Party opposes POFMA Bill
sections.summary: The Workers' Party opposes the Bill while agreeing legislation is needed against online falsehoods, foreign election influence and social divide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party (WP) opposes the POFMA Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We agree that it is necessary to legislate to deal with those who use online falsehoods to destabilise our current political system and multiracial society, to prevent foreigners from influencing election results through the Internet, and to order tech companies to take down remarks which could cause social divide.

sections.label: Motive to deter social media critics
sections.summary: The passage states that the underlying motive is to deter critics on social media.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The underlying motive is, in fact, to deter critics on the social media.

sections.label: Minister power over falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill lets the Minister decide what are falsehoods and what punishment to mete out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, this Bill allows the Minister to have absolute power to decide what are falsehoods and what punishment to mete out.

sections.label: Election official conflict of interest
sections.summary: The Bill requires the Minister to appoint a Government official during elections, but the passage asks who ensures this official will not harm public interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Although the Bill stipulates that during an election, the Minister must appoint a Government official to perform the duties on behalf of the Minister to avoid conflicts of interests, who can ensure that this Government official will not do things that could harm public interests to benefit himself and the Minister?

sections.label: WP rejects Minister judging punishment
sections.summary: The WP cannot accept the Minister judging and deciding punishment, and believes the Minister should first prove falsity and ill-intent to the Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In a word, the WP cannot accept that the Bill empowers the Minister to judge and decide how to mete out punishment, when it is a basic right concerning people’s freedom to comment on politics.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP believes that the Minister should complain to the Court first and prove to the judges that the news published online is false and there is ill-intent behind the news.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, clause 2 stipulates that the Government has power to deal with misleading remarks, but what is the dividing line between misleading and false statement?

sections.label: Information or opinion example
sections.summary: The passage asks whether saying the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages are to buy votes is information or opinion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, if I say the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages are to buy votes, is this considered information or opinion?

sections.label: Court as final judge
sections.summary: The passage states that although the Government says the Court will be the final judge, this may be so theoretically.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Although the Government says that the Court will be the final judge, this may be so theoretically.

sections.label: High threshold for applying law
sections.summary: The passage states the threshold for applying this law is necessarily very high and should not stymie public discourse and debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The threshold for the application of this law is necessarily very high, as it should be.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: We should not allow this law to stymie public discourse, robust debate and the growth and flourishing of contested views.

sections.label: State duty to reduce falsehoods
sections.summary: The state has a public duty to reduce falsehoods because two assumptions are largely false.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Given that these two assumptions are largely false, the state has a public duty to reduce falsehoods.

sections.label: Law alone cannot protect trust
sections.summary: Protecting trust in institutions and democratic discourse is conceit if seen as the law's preserve alone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Given this limited application of the law, the ambition to protect trust in our institutions and democratic discourse is mere conceit if we conceive of it as being the preserve of the law alone.

sections.label: Resolve to use extra-legal means
sections.summary: The speaker asks the House to record its resolve to respond to falsehoods through extra-legal means.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: What I would ask of all of us in this House is to record our resolve to respond to the rise of such falsehoods through extra-legal means.

sections.label: Calibrated toolkit against disinformation
sections.summary: The legislation takes its bearing from the SC's recommendation and provides a calibrated toolkit, using Correction Directions sparingly to offer facts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Today, we continue to see the use of bots and avatar accounts to spread falsehoods and amplify viewpoints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: This piece of legislation must take its bearing from the SC’s recommendation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Sometimes, we do not know; sometimes, we cannot decide what is false or true.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: This piece of legislation is a scalpel, not a sledgehammer, as it provides a calibrated toolkit to address the problem of disinformation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In terms of the tools to address falsehoods, most of the time, we will use Correction Directions which will be used sparingly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: These "Correction Directions" are a unique remedy, whose purpose is not to censor content, but to provide a broader range of facts for the public to consider.

sections.label: Few takedown orders under POFMA
sections.summary: Even if POFMA were in operation today, the law's drafting means there would be very few takedown orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Even if POFMA had been in operation today, given the way the law has been drafted, there would have been very few takedown orders.

sections.label: New Bill as new treatment
sections.summary: The new Bill is a new treatment to deal with a new virus, and treatment cannot be delayed by fear.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: We cannot delay treatment just because we are afraid of seeing a doctor.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: This new Bill is, therefore, a new treatment to deal with this new "virus".

sections.label: New Bill and online falsehoods
sections.summary: The new Bill plugs a gap left by 23-year-old legislation, making Correction Orders the main tool against online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Earlier, Mr Low Thia Khiang said he does not believe that the new Bill has given less authority to the Minister.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: But the Minister had explained earlier that existing legislation in Singapore, such as the Broadcasting Act, was implemented 23 years ago.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Back then, there was no social media or large-scale Internet platforms.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Therefore, we did not have legislation that target online falsehoods specifically, which is a new kind of "virus", and this new Bill does the job of plugging the gap.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Under existing legislation, blocking out content is the primary measure taken.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: However, the Minister has explained that under the new Bill, Correction Orders would be the main tool used to clarify false information.

sections.label: Bill targets deliberate falsehood purveyors
sections.summary: The new Bill is not targeted at ordinary folks but at purveyors of deliberate online falsehoods detrimental to public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Here, there is a need to clarify that this new Bill is not targeted at ordinary folks but purveyors of deliberate online falsehoods that are detrimental to public interest.

sections.label: Parliament monitors the Minister
sections.summary: The new Bill monitors the Minister on three fronts, including Parliament questioning and published takedown directives, to prevent abuse of power.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Thirdly, he is monitored by Parliament as Members can also question the Minister's decision.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: If the Minister requests that certain information be taken down, this directive will also be published.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Therefore, the new Bill monitors the Minister on three fronts to ensure that he does not abuse his power and that the process is, indeed, in the public interest.

sections.label: Public interest not specified
sections.summary: The Bill does not specify what constitutes public interest because every instance harming public interest cannot be imagined.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: The Bill does not specify what constitute public interest as we cannot possibly imagine every instance that will harm public interest.

sections.label: Checks on executive powers
sections.summary: Various checks and balances within the new Bill keep the Government's executive powers in check.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Various checks and balances have been put in place within this new Bill to ensure that the Government's executive powers remain in check.

sections.label: Minister decides public interest
sections.summary: The Minister decides what is public interest, falsehood and action, since public interest is not clearly stipulated in the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: Under this Bill, even though in theory, you can go to the Court and question the Minister’s interpretation of the text, and say that it is wrong to issue the correction or takedown order, but before that, the Minister would have arrived at his own conclusion and made a decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: Besides, public interest is up to the individual's interpretation as it is not clearly stipulated in the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: Therefore, it is all up to the Minister to decide what is in the public interest, what is falsehood, and what he will do about it.

sections.label: Minister lodging complaint in Court
sections.summary: The passage states that going to Court is not simple, so the Minister should lodge a complaint and let the judge decide.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: Even though you can go to Court and there is a procedure, things are not so simple.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: So, we believe that the correct way is for the Minister to lodge a complaint in Court and let the judge decide.

sections.label: Chinese character and Court adjudicator
sections.summary: The speaker says the Member interpreted the character "众" differently, and states the Court is the ultimate adjudicator of falsehood.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: When I spoke about the Chinese character "众" (zhong) or "public", I meant to talk about everyone working together, but the Member insisted on interpreting the character "众" (zhong) as being made up of a big character "人" (ren) or "person" on top.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: I have stated clearly that the Court is the ultimate adjudicator for what is considered falsehood.

sections.label: Public interest in new Bill
sections.summary: The passage says Low Thia Khiang found "public interest" inadequately explained, but it is covered in existing legislation and examples in the new Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: Mr Low Thia Khiang also says that "public interest" was not adequately explained in the new Bill, and he is uncomfortable with that.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: However, I would like to clarify that "public interest" is already covered in existing legislation, and many examples have also been included in the new Bill, so the principles and possible scenarios have been laid out.

sections.label: Committee submissions on online falsehoods
sections.summary: The Committee, appointed in January 2018, called for public views on deliberate online falsehoods and received 170 submissions from various people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Committee was appointed in January 2018 and subsequently called for members of the public to submit their thoughts on the causes and consequences of deliberate online falsehoods and suggest countermeasures against the threat.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: We received 170 submissions from people from all walks of life, including academics, community leaders, think tanks, students and other individuals.

sections.label: Committee report and recommendations
sections.summary: The Committee deliberated almost six months and produced a 176-page report with 22 recommendations, including new legislation to disrupt online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Committee deliberated on the matter over a period of almost six months and eventually produced a 176-page report, not inclusive of the annexes, with 22 recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: One of the key thrusts of the recommendations was to disrupt online falsehoods through new legislation which would empower the Government to take the necessary action.

sections.label: Singaporeans active social media users
sections.summary: A Business Times report stated 70% of Singaporeans are active social media users on mobile devices, double the global average of 34%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: A Business Times report stated that 70% of Singaporeans are active social media users on mobile devices, double the global average of 34%.

sections.label: State-sponsored disinformation against Singapore
sections.summary: The Committee received evidence in private hearings that State-sponsored disinformation operations have been carried out against Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In fact, in private hearings, the Committee received evidence that State-sponsored disinformation operations have been carried out against Singapore.

sections.label: Calls to stem online falsehoods
sections.summary: Many representors, experts and laypersons, called for measures to swiftly stem online falsehoods, citing speed of irreparable damage.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: A significant number of representors, both experts and laypersons, called for measures to swiftly stem the spread of online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: They were of the view that such measures are vital because of the speed at which online falsehoods can cause irreparable damage.

sections.label: Correction, takedown and court challenge
sections.summary: Government can direct correction or takedown of falsehoods, and a person who disagrees can go to Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Government can issue a direction for a correction alongside the falsehood or, in more extreme situations, for the falsehood to be taken down.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: However, if a person disagrees with the direction, he can go to Court to obtain a determination.

sections.label: Criminal consequences for deliberate acts
sections.summary: Only those who act deliberately will face criminal consequences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Only those who act deliberately will face criminal consequences.

sections.label: Tripartite model against online falsehoods
sections.summary: A tripartite model of Government, media and technology companies and media literate consumers can tackle online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Indeed, borrowing from the experience of our Labour Movement with its tripartite model comprising the Government, employers and workers, we can foster an innovative tripartite model for tackling online falsehoods, one that comprises the Government, media and technology companies as well as media literate consumers.

sections.label: Advisory panel for ministerial directions
sections.summary: A panel of experts from technology industry and media consumers should advise the Minister on issuing directions.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The execution of targeted or general corrections will differ from platform to platform, translating into varying degrees of consumer exposure to the corrections, and with varying levels of effectiveness.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would thus like to propose that if the Minister must retain the authority to issue directions expeditiously, he or she should be advised by a panel of experts representing the technology industry and media consumers, somewhat like the Film Consultative Panel.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In other words, the Minister should have, at his disposal, the wisdom of an advisory panel that can determine whether a particular course of action is realistic or practical, or whether it could be counterproductive.

sections.label: Information Integrity Institute proposal
sections.summary: A proposed Information Integrity Institute, funded by media and technology companies, would fact-check and host verifications of falsehoods to supplement POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Going beyond POFMA for the longer term, in order to better align with the democratised nature of our media environment, we should further concretise this tripartite approach to tackling online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We should establish what I call an Information Integrity Institute, or ICube for short, to supplement POFMA's correction regime.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It should be funded by contributions from all media and technology companies.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: ICube will play a critical fact-checking role and develop the expertise to do so swiftly and effectively.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It can host an online repository of verifications of falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Over time, it should develop a reputation as a reliable third-party fact checker that is the first port of call for consumers in need of authentication.

sections.label: Shared funding and legislative monitoring
sections.summary: Shared funding would make ICube less liable to partisanship allegations, and unintended effects of legislative approaches must be monitored and amended.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Due to its shared funding, ICube will be less liable to attract allegations of partisanship, and, therefore, more likely to engender trust in its determinations of truth and falsity, and the verifications and refutations which it issues.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In light of these shifting complexities, the possible unintended effects of legislative approaches to addressing falsehoods must be closely monitored and amended if necessary.

sections.label: WP on POFMA arbiter
sections.summary: The WP disagrees with POFMA giving Ministers first-arbiter powers and suggests the Judiciary become the first arbiter instead.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP disagrees with the basic principle of POFMA which provides powers to the Ministers, that is, the Executive, as the first arbiter in deciding whether a remark or statement can be considered as a falsehood or otherwise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP suggests that the Judiciary, and not the Executive, become the first arbiter.

sections.label: Definition of false statement
sections.summary: Clause 2 defines a false statement as one that is false or not false but misleading, and the word misleading raises abuse-of-power concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Clause 2 provides the definition that a false statement is a statement that is indeed false, or one that is not false but can be misleading.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The word “misleading” in this definition raises concerns about the possibility of abuse of power taking place.

sections.label: Shanmugam no assurances
sections.summary: Minister Shanmugam said he could not give any assurances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Minister Shanmugam said that he could not give any assurances.

sections.label: Second key and abuse of power
sections.summary: A second key aims to prevent an irresponsible government using Reserves for political benefit, and the Courts as sole arbiter would remove abuse-of-power concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The objective of having a second key is to prevent an irresponsible government from using the Reserves as they please for political benefit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is rather surprising as to why there is a difference and inconsistency in the Government's approach and values when dealing with the possibility of abuse of power between the POFMA issue and the national Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is because if the Courts become the sole arbiter, there will be no concerns about abuse of power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As I have said earlier in my speech, if there is abuse of power, it will undermine social cohesion and this runs counter to the primary objective of having a law to deal with online falsehoods and manipulation.

sections.label: Motion of amendment to Bill
sections.summary: Three members submitted a Motion of amendment to the Bill, vetted by the Attorney-General's Chambers, to add discipline while retaining Government ability to deal with online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, Ms Irene Quay and I submitted a Motion of amendment to this Bill as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The proposed amendments seek to mitigate these concerns by ensuring there is discipline in the way the Act would be utilised while ensuring that the Government has the ability to deal with the full range of threats posed by deliberate online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The proposed amendments were, as part of our robust Parliamentary process, vetted by the Attorney-General's Chambers.

sections.label: MOM fact-check press releases
sections.summary: MOM issued 21 corrective newsroom releases called Fact Checks since September 2017, 18 addressing NGO-published content about MOM's priorities, processes and practice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: For instance, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has issued a total of 21 newsroom releases of a corrective nature that it refers to as "Fact Checks" since September 2017.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Eighteen of those 21 "fact-checking" press releases, addressed NGO-published content about MOM's priorities, processes and practice.

sections.label: Public interest definition concern
sections.summary: Clause 4(f) is broadly worded, raising concern that any criticism of the Government could be considered a statement diminishing public confidence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Section 4 of the Bill defines, I quote, "public interest" and the circumstances under which it is justified to take action.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: However, clause 4(f) is again broadly worded and states: "action is justified under the Bill if the falsehood would prevent a diminution of public confidence in the Government, an Organ of State, a Statutory Board, or a part of the Government, an Organ of State or a Statutory Board".

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The concern is, with such an overreaching scope coupled with the broad and subjective definition of "fact" and "false", that any criticism of the Government could be considered a statement that would diminish public confidence, as stated in the Bill.

sections.label: Explaining each Direction issued
sections.summary: For each Direction issued, the Government should publicly explain evidence of the falsehood, the public interest objectives, and why the Direction is suitable.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Would her posts be targeted because they contributed to a wave of diminished public confidence in the Government?

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: This means that for each Direction that has been issued, the Government should publicly explain or demonstrate three things: (a) evidence that demonstrates the falsehood, or the evidence setting forth the true facts; (b) the public interest objectives of this Direction, and (c) why this Direction is suitable to achieve those public interest objectives.

sections.label: SC countermeasures and proposed council
sections.summary: The SC report listed five areas of proposed countermeasures, and the speakers propose an independent council called the Independent Council on Online Falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The SC's report listed five areas of proposed countermeasures: (a) nurture an informed public; (b) reinforce social trust and cohesion; (c) promote fact-checking, (d) disrupt online falsehoods; and (e) deal with threats to national security and sovereignty.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: We propose that an independent council be set up to give effect to these SC recommendations to be called the Independent Council on Online Falsehoods.

sections.label: Independent Council appointment proposal
sections.summary: The Independent Council on Online Falsehoods is proposed like the National Council on Problem Gambling, with members appointed by a Select Committee of Parliament, not a Minister.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The impetus to set up the Independent Council on Online Falsehoods is the same as that of the National Council on Problem Gambling: a recognition that a dedicated independent council is best suited to undertake the national responsibility of assessing the impact of a new legislation and significant development for the country and providing specific expertise to advise the Government on the effectiveness of current measures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: However, Mr Speaker, I would like to highlight that unlike councils stipulated in other legislation, we are proposing that members of the Council are to be appointed by a Select Committee of Parliament, not by a Minister.

sections.label: National information and media literacy framework
sections.summary: Minister Iswaran announced a national information and media literacy framework to be launched by June 2019, developed by MCI, NLB, IMDA and CSA, with MOE rolling out a New Media Literacy toolkit to schools.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Minister Iswaran has announced that a national framework to build information and media literacy will be launched by June 2019, jointly developed by the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI), the National Library Board (NLB), the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) will also be rolling out a New Media Literacy toolkit to all primary and secondary schools, as well as junior colleges.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: If I may, Mr Speaker, I would like to request that all Singaporeans be given a review of all exercise of powers under the Bill by way of a Ministerial Statement in Parliament a year from the implementation of the Act after the Bill is passed, with the findings and recommendations from the Independent Council on Online Falsehoods.

sections.label: Reviewing existing harsher laws
sections.summary: The Bill scopes down Government powers compared to existing laws like the Broadcasting Act and Telecoms Act, and the Government is urged to review these harsher laws.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: As the Minister has shared, this Bill seeks to scope down and calibrate the Government’s powers compared to existing laws, including the Broadcasting Act, Telecoms Act and so on.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: I would, therefore, sincerely urge the Government to consider reviewing these existing harsher laws to honour the intent with this Bill of scoping down executive powers.

sections.label: Foreign falsehoods and democratic vulnerability
sections.summary: Falsehoods are deliberately created by foreign state actors to subvert governments and electoral processes, as shown by fake news in the US Presidential Election and Brexit vote.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Falsehoods are deliberately created, for example, by foreign state actors to interfere with and subvert governments and electoral processes in other countries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The fact that the US Presidential Election and the Brexit vote involved significant amounts of fake news being circulated and relied on by voters shows that even the most advanced democracies are vulnerable to this threat.

sections.label: Judiciary versus Executive decision
sections.summary: The main difference of opinion is that some believe the Judiciary should decide first and issue directions rather than the Executive, while the Bill envisions a competent authority because fake news is prevalent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Their main difference of opinion is that they believe the Judiciary should make the decision first and issue directions, rather than the Executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: What the Bill envisions is a competent authority because fake news is a relatively prevalent problem.

sections.label: Powers against false amplifiers and websites
sections.summary: The Bill includes powers against false amplifiers and fake news websites, in addition to what is likely the most commonly used tool.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Of course, this is likely to be the most commonly used tool.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But there are also interesting powers included in the Bill which includes powers against false amplifiers and fake news websites.

sections.label: Judicial scrutiny at the end
sections.summary: Judicial scrutiny at the end is effective and logical because the authority decides first, the Minister reviews, and improper decisions face scrutiny by the Judiciary and public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: That would be a complete abuse of the judicial process, a waste of resources and ineffective against the threat.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But the system of having judicial scrutiny at the end, I think, is actually very effective and very logical, because, in a sense, the authority decides first, the Minister has a chance to review, and if the Minister makes an improper decision, that would be under scrutiny by the Judiciary and by the public in that process.

sections.label: Nominated Members' amendment on checks
sections.summary: An amendment by Nominated Members adds many checks; the speaker welcomes some points but finds other mechanisms, including a council, unnecessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: There is also an amendment filed by some of our friends, the Nominated Members of Parliament, which include a large number of additional checks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I am grateful they put so much thought into the process and some of the points are well made, in particular, the one about the Minister having to make the decision quickly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I think this is going to be captured in the subsidiary legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But with the greatest of respect to my friends, I do not think a lot of the other mechanisms are probably necessary, including the setting up of a council.

sections.label: No statutory body needed
sections.summary: The speaker says academics or information access and parliamentary questions can achieve the objective without setting up another statutory body.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I think that can equally well be done by academics or people who have access to the information, and questions in Parliament can be filed about decisions made by the Minister, how many have been made, and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: So, I do not think we need to set up another body by statute to achieve this objective.

sections.label: Court decisions in hot situations
sections.summary: The speaker says it is unnecessary for the Court to decide, especially in hot situations like elections with hundreds of articles daily.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: My view is that it is unnecessary for the Court to do so and, especially if you are in a "hot" situation, say, largely, elections, as has happened in the US and in Europe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: You have hundreds of articles a day; how are the judges going to come in and make a decision?

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: Is the Executive supposed to come in and take out a hundred applications and then get the respondent for each one?

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: It is far better if they can just make the decision and get it done.

sections.label: Frequency of exercising powers
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the powers may be exercised several hundred times daily, depending on the volume of attack.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Does the hon Member envisage that these powers are likely to be exercised several hundred times every day?

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: It may have to be, depending on the volume of attack we come under.

sections.label: Appeal grounds for Directions
sections.summary: For Part 3 and 4 Directions, appeals to the High Court may only set aside a Direction on three grounds; the Minister's opinion and clause 4 definitions cannot be decided.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For Part 3 and 4 Directions, a person who has been served with a Correction or stop Direction, may appeal to the High Court against the Directions after having first applied to the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: However, for both Part 3 and Part 4 Directions, the appeal provisions expressly provide that the High Court may only set aside such a Direction on three grounds of appeal as seen in clauses 17(5) and 29(5).

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The issue of whether the Minister was correct or not in arriving in his opinion that it is in the public interest to issue the Direction itself does not come within the three grounds of appeal and cannot be decided by the Court on appeal under clause 17 or 29.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Similarly, the exact meaning and coverage of the definitions provided in clause 4 cannot be decided by the Court hearing an appeal under clause 17 or 29.

sections.label: Public interest definition in clause 4(f)
sections.summary: Clause 4(f) defines doing anything in the public interest as preventing a diminution of public confidence in Government, Organ of state or Statutory Board duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Still on clause 4 of the Bill, clause 4(f) provides for one definition of doing anything in the public interest if the doing is to prevent a diminution of public confidence in the performance of any duty or function of, or in the exercise of any power by the Government, an Organ of state, a Statutory Board and so on.
