sentences.text: We did not do any database check but, to the best of MOE's knowledge, 71 are foreign academics based in foreign universities and 52 are Singaporeans – 25 based in foreign universities outside of Singapore and 27 based in local universities.

sections.label: Two gates for falsehoods
sections.summary: The speaker reiterates the two gates any falsehood must pass before correction or removal under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: First, let me reiterate, the two gates through which any falsehood must pass before it can be corrected or removed by this Bill.

sections.label: Third gate for criminal liability
sections.summary: Criminal liability requires a third gate: the propagator must know the falsehood is false and harmful.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: For there to be criminal liability, a third gate has to be crossed, which is that the propagator of the falsehood must have knowledge that it is false and it is harmful.

sections.label: Turkey EU referendum falsehood
sections.summary: During the referendum campaign, a falsehood circulated that Turkey would join the EU and Britain would be flooded with Turkish immigrants.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: During the campaign on the referendum, a falsehood was going around that Turkey was going to join the European Union (EU) and Britain would be flooded with immigrants from Turkey.

sections.label: Targets of the Bill
sections.summary: The Bill targets deliberate lies, connivance, impersonations, and incitement of unrest and societal anger and turmoil.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Deliberate lies, connivance, impersonations, incitement of unrest and societal anger and turmoil.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: This is the world of online falsehoods and manipulations that this Bill is targeting.

sections.label: Research on data and hypotheses
sections.summary: Researchers gathered data from Government departments, tested hypotheses, and found HDB flat prices rose after KTM Railway removal and yellow taxis had fewer accidents than blue taxis.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: They gathered vast amounts of data, including getting a lot of data from Government departments and agencies, and tested many hypotheses.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: They found that after the removal of the Keretapi Tanah Melayu (KTM) Railway, the price of HDB flats around the railway line went up significantly.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: They found out that yellow taxis have fewer accidents than blue taxis.

sections.label: First gate falsehood question
sections.summary: At the first gate, the question of falsehood is answered no because researchers used real data and observations for their conclusions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: At the first gate, you ask, "Is there falsehood?" No, because researchers used real data and observations to draw their conclusions.

sections.label: Bill on truthfulness of facts
sections.summary: The Bill concerns truthfulness of facts, with Minister Shanmugam to explain why and how, citing examples of alleged assaults, a presidential speech and Turkey joining the EU.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: I am sure Minister Shanmugam will explain why and how.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: This Bill is about truthfulness of "facts" – did the men really assault the women, did the President really give that speech, was Turkey really joining the EU?

sections.label: Commitment to science and evidence
sections.summary: The speaker assures the House that for empirical research, they will stay true to science and empirical evidence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In our context, I can assure the House, that if it is empirical research, we will stay true to science and empirical evidence.

sections.label: POFMA and false research data
sections.summary: POFMA does not apply in such discourse unless research uses false observations and fabricated data, which prevents proper public discourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Under both scenarios, POFMA does not apply in such a discourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The only way POFMA comes in is if the research uses false observations and data to start with, you fabricated the data, which prevents public discourse from taking place properly.

sections.label: Activists expressing opinions
sections.summary: Any activist will not be caught by POFMA if they express an opinion or hurl criticisms at the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Any activist will not be caught by POFMA if you express an opinion or even hurl criticisms at the Government.

sections.label: POFMA covers online falsehood spreaders
sections.summary: Any activist using the online medium to spread falsehoods and harm society will come under POFMA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Conversely, any activist, whether you are an academic or a man or woman on the street who uses the online medium to spread falsehoods and harm society, will come under POFMA.

sections.label: POFMA and democratic discourse
sections.summary: POFMA enhances, and not diminishes, democratic public discourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: POFMA enhances, and not diminishes, democratic public discourse.

sections.label: Falsehoods spread faster than truth
sections.summary: Today's falsehoods differ from the past because they can spread six times faster than the truth.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: However, the falsehoods of today are different from those of the past.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: That is, falsehoods can spread six times faster than the truth.

sections.label: Bill goals and boundaries
sections.summary: There is a responsibility to find solutions to rectify these problems, and the Bill has clear goals and defined boundaries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We have the responsibility to find solutions to rectify these problems.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: This Bill has clear goals and defined boundaries.

sections.label: Bill scope and targets
sections.summary: The Bill applies only to the examples mentioned, covers facts not opinions, and targets writers of fake news, not spreaders.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The Bill is only applicable to the examples mentioned, covering facts and not opinions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Furthermore, the Bill targets the writers of fake news and not the people who spread it.

sections.label: Online falsehoods effects listed
sections.summary: Online falsehoods have affected election and referendum results, twisted public sentiments, heightened tensions and altered political discourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, we know that online falsehoods have affected election and referendum results, twisted public sentiments, heightened public tensions, societal tensions and altered the political discourse.

sections.label: New Zealand shooting Facebook feed
sections.summary: The New Zealand shooter had a live Facebook feed lasting 17 minutes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In the recent shooting in New Zealand, the shooter had a live Facebook feed for 17 minutes.

sections.label: POFMA cannot remove live feed
sections.summary: Because the feed was live, POFMA cannot enforce a takedown of it.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: For it was live; it was what took place.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: So, POFMA cannot enforce a takedown of this feed.

sections.label: POFMA Correction order powers
sections.summary: For online falsehoods, POFMA gives the Government powers for surgical insertion of additional facts via a Correction order.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: When online falsehoods are perpetrated, it only gives the Government legislative powers for a surgical and judicious insertion of additional facts, through a Correction order.

sections.label: POFMA response to technological change
sections.summary: POFMA is a necessary response to technological change, to protect democratic public discourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: While small, POFMA is a necessary response to this tectonic technological change, to protect democratic public discourse which we cherish.

sections.label: Economists' data and jobs claim
sections.summary: Economists relied on data the Government later called incomplete, asserting one of four jobs went to residents, while actually nine of 10 did.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: If I recall the facts of that case, the economists have relied on some data which later the Government said was incomplete and they had asserted based on the data that out of four jobs that was created, only one job went to a Singapore resident and three jobs went to the intake of foreigners.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: In actual fact, out of 10 jobs, nine went to residents.

sections.label: Researchers' conclusions and POFMA
sections.summary: The economists' conclusion was based on incomplete but not fabricated data, and their opinion is not part of POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Their conclusion that most of the jobs went to foreigners, that is the conclusion of the study.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: What they based that conclusion on was on data, although incomplete, was not fabricated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: And as for the conclusion that most jobs went to foreigners, that was their conclusion and their opinion, which is also not part of POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, so long as researchers abide by research discipline, I do not see how they can be caught by POFMA unless they fabricated data.

sections.label: Pre-POFMA correction by Manpower Minister
sections.summary: The speaker reads a Channel NewsAsia article quoting then Manpower Minister Ng Eng Hen criticising NTU academics' figures as a pre-POFMA correction.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The first one is: I am not so sure that the characterisation that what the two economists said would not have come under POFMA because there was some kind of correction that was done in 2003.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: And I am going to just read off the Channel NewsAsia article which quotes the then Minister of Manpower Dr Ng Eng Hen who said, "If your figures are wrong, it is irresponsible, unprofessional to put up those figures.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I do not know how they got their figures and what their methods are", said Dr Ng Eng Hen.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: And he added that, "The NTU academics had not consulted the Manpower Ministry or the Department of Statistics." So, that is as good as a correction, I think, in a pre-POFMA era.

sections.label: Disagreement versus POFMA falsehood
sections.summary: The speaker says the Manpower Minister disagreed with the research report, which does not mean POFMA would apply, and distinguishes research from activism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: But it is obvious that the Manpower Minister then did not agree with the conclusion of the research report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: That does not equal to it being caught under POFMA today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: That is why I differentiated between research and activism; that, even when POFMA does not apply to research, please expect us, if we do not agree with the outcome, to present other data, present our arguments and try to correct public perceptions, and try to convince the public otherwise.

sections.label: Ministries tightening language on falsehoods
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Minister asks colleagues or Ministries to tighten their language so people do not mistake disagreements for falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
sentences.text: And I would hope that the Minister would have some views on, maybe asking his colleagues or Ministries to tighten up a bit in their language, so that people do not inadvertently think things are false when they are actually not.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: That is one value of this discourse that we have in this Chamber, that we are now a lot more careful in defining what is a disagreement and what is a falsehood.

sections.label: Falsehoods causing violence in Myanmar, Indonesia, Sri Lanka
sections.summary: The passage lists falsehoods said to have caused violence in Myanmar in 2014, Indonesia in 2016 and Sri Lanka in 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2014, Myanmar witnessed two days of violence leaving two dead and dozens injured, with mosques being burnt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It was caused by a falsehood from a Buddhist woman who was paid to make false rape claims against two Muslim brothers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2016, 12 Buddhist temples in northern Sumatra of Indonesia were plundered and burnt down by a Muslim mob in 24 hours with billions of rupiah in losses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Again, it was caused by a falsehood that a Chinese woman had complained about noise from a mosque, threw items at it, expelled the prayer leader and disrupted prayers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Just last year, in 2018, Sri Lanka witnessed widespread ethnic violence with mosques burnt, people attacked and the government declaring a State of Emergency and temporarily banning social media platforms.

sections.label: German states targeting bots spreading falsehoods
sections.summary: Justice ministers in three German states proposed using anti-botnet legislation against automated accounts spreading online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Justice ministers in three German states have proposed using anti-botnet legislation to crack down on automated social media accounts, or "bots", which spread online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Botnets are suspected to have engineered voter sentiments during recent events, such as the UK EU membership referendum and the 2016 US elections.

sections.label: Deepfakes and POFMA Bill powers
sections.summary: The speaker raises deepfakes and urges the Government to watch emerging technologies, but says the POFMA Bill's powers are not acceptable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One area of concern I would like to raise in this House is the issue of deepfakes which will increasingly become a problem, as highlighted by the Minister earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In order to successfully tackle the problem, I urge the Government to keep an eye out for emerging disruptive technologies, such as deep learning and generative adversarial networks (GANs), which make it possible to manipulate images and videos so well that it becomes difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish false from authentic ones.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In fact, apps like FakeApp and Lyrebird have made the production of "deepfakes" accessible to anyone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am confident that the Government will place peace, harmony and the safety of Singapore at its heart and do the best as Singaporeans and for Singaporeans and be counted upon to steward these considerable powers in a fair, consistent and thoughtful manner, consistent with our democratic values and our duty to protect Singaporeans from the ill-effects of online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: But this POFMA Bill gives the government of the day massive targeted powers that go far beyond this remit and is, therefore, not acceptable and not good for Singapore in the long run.

sections.label: Misleading term and interpretations
sections.summary: The speaker says adding "misleading" opens truth to multiple interpretations and asks if Government can quote a statement out of context and accuse them of misleading the public.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: To add the term "misleading" here is dangerous, as it opens up the judgement of truth to multiple interpretations of connotations and implications.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: By this definition, a statement can become misleading by virtue of being interpreted in the worst possible way, whether wholly or in part, whether on its own or in context.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: So, does this mean that the Government can take a statement I make, quote a part of it out of context, choose the worst of all the possible interpretations of the partial statement taken out of context, and then accuse me of misleading the public on a matter of public interest?

sections.label: Objection to public confidence definition
sections.summary: The speaker objects to sub-definition (f) on public confidence in Government performance, saying it makes any disputed critical statement of fact liable to the law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: I have reservations about (d) with regard to elections but I will focus on (f).

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: I object to (f) which has to do with public confidence in the performance of the Government.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: This sub-definition makes any disputed statement of fact that merely risks reducing some public confidence in the performance of any action by just a part of the Government and Statutory Boards liable to this law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: This is practically any statement of fact critical of the Government.

sections.label: CPF payout age online furore
sections.summary: The speaker cites a public online furore over claims the Government quietly raised the CPF payout eligibility age from 65 to 70.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The first is the case at the beginning of this year when there was a public online furore over claims that the Government had quietly raised the CPF payout eligibility age from 65 to 70 years old.

sections.label: Police preferential treatment accusation
sections.summary: The speaker cites a case accusing the Police of preferential treatment for letting off a male undergraduate who filmed a woman in an NUS Hall shower.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The second is the recent case accusing the Police of preferential treatment for letting off a male undergraduate for filming a woman in the shower in an NUS Hall of Residence because the student’s parents were well-connected to powerful people.

sections.label: Police praise and earned confidence
sections.summary: The speaker says the Police earned public praise by respecting the offender's privacy and getting family permission, showing public confidence must be earned, not enforced.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: Furthermore, the way the Police went about dispelling the falsehood earned praise from the public, as the Police respected the privacy of the offender and obtained permission from his family to reveal their background.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: These two examples show us that public confidence in the performance of the Government has to be earned and cannot be enforced.

sections.label: Leave truth arbitration to Courts
sections.summary: The speaker says the law sets the tone for generations and believes truth arbitration should be left to the Courts, not a thin-skinned Executive.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: This law is an important one because it will set the tone for generations to come.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: I believe, as do my WP colleagues, that it is best to leave the arbitration of truths to the Courts and not have the Executive of the Government sullied in mudfights with the public over falsehoods, and worse, leave Singapore society wide open to abuses by a thin-skinned Executive protecting its own institutional interests.

sections.label: Co-correction versus ministerial correction
sections.summary: The Government should co-correct with the informed public rather than correct falsehoods unilaterally by Ministerial fiat, and should not be the referee.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The Government should focus on co-correction with the informed public, not the unilateral correction of falsehoods by Ministerial fiat.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: It is a star player in the football team, the captain even, but it should not be the referee.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: I do not agree with the very notion that the Courts are the final arbiter of truth in this law, because this means that the Executive of the Government is the initial arbiter of truth.

sections.label: Speed without executive arbitral powers
sections.summary: The need for speed in exigent matters can be met by speeding up Court applications without giving the Executive arbitral powers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The argument to give the Executive these draconian powers of forcing the truth on the public is that the Executive needs speed to act quickly when it comes to exigent matters of public interest.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: But there is no reason why the process of applying to the Court for corrections and takedowns cannot be sped up.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The need for speed in certain areas can be met without misplacing arbitral powers in the Executive.

sections.label: Courts arbitrating disputed truths
sections.summary: The Judiciary enacts justice by arbitrating disputed truths, and protection from online falsehoods should lie with the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: The Judiciary enacts justice by arbitrating disputed truths.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
sentences.text: It is clear that the protection of society and the Government from online falsehoods should lie with the Courts.

sections.label: Unpacking laws on responsible speech
sections.summary: Several laws target different kinds of harmful speech, and it is important to unpack for people what constitutes responsible speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: What people do not understand is that there are several laws, each targeting different kinds of harmful speech with remedies that vary in strength.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: These laws include (a) POFMA and POHA; (b) the Penal Code, sections 298 and 298A; (c) Sedition Act: sections 3, 4; (d) Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act: section 8; and (e) Contempt of Court: sections on scandalising of Courts, and subjudice contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: These laws are complex to understand by themselves, and it is even harder for most Singaporeans to understand how it works altogether.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Therefore, it is very important that we unpack for our people, in simple terms, what constitutes responsible speech: (a) the various laws; (b) the principles behind these laws; (c) our unique circumstances and vulnerabilities; and (d) who are these laws meant for?

sections.label: Reasonable excuse for intermediaries
sections.summary: The law provides a defence of reasonable excuse for Internet intermediaries, raising whether an intermediary can decline to comply if it hurts profits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under the law, there is a defence of "reasonable excuse" for the Internet intermediaries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Does this mean that an intermediary can choose not to comply and invoke the defence, if it hurts their profits to comply?

sections.label: Fake news and healthy discourse
sections.summary: What matters is not only ensuring fake news has no place in Singapore but also that laws do not curtail healthy discourse or diminish the marketplace of ideas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Because what matters is not just ensuring that fake news has no place in Singapore, but also to ensure that our laws do not unintentionally curtail healthy and necessary discourse or diminish the marketplace of ideas that healthy democracies, like Singapore, require.

sections.label: Minister Shanmugam on corrections and appeals
sections.summary: Minister Shanmugam said corrections or takedowns apply only to factual falsehoods undermining public interest, with court challenge and an easy, affordable appeal process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: Yesterday, Minister Shanmugam gave a detailed statement, and that corrections or takedowns should only be made if it is a factual falsehood and undermines public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: And the Minister's decision can be challenged in Court and changed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: In addition, the appeal process is also made easy and affordable.

sections.label: Need for tools against falsehoods
sections.summary: These have far-reaching impacts on countries and citizens, and effective tools are needed now to deal with drip-feed falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: These have far-reaching impacts on countries, as well as their citizens.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: We need effective tools to deal with drip-feed falsehoods and we need them right now.

sections.label: Oversight mechanism and public reasons
sections.summary: Regular accessible content can cause a drip-feed of falsehoods and loss of public confidence, so Minister Shanmugam clarified a clear oversight mechanism, with reasons and evidence released publicly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: Yet, if such content is made accessible on a regular basis, this potentially leads to a drip-feed of falsehoods and diminution of public confidence over time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: I am assured to know that Minister Shanmugam had clarified that there would be a "clear oversight mechanism" in place to prevent possible abuse of power by the Singapore Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: In doing so, reasons and evidence should also be released to the public upon issuance of the takedown or correction order.

sections.label: Transparency, timeliness and regular reviews
sections.summary: The Minister acknowledges transparency's importance, but timeliness of publishing corrections matters, and regular reviews should assess what content becomes fake news and why.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: I am glad that the Minister acknowledges the importance of transparency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: However, the timeliness of publishing the correction is also important, and I urge the Minister to consider this factor as well and, if possible, tighten the time needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: Regular reviews should be done to assess what type of content is prone to being turned into fake news content, and what are the reasons, and what can we do about it.

sections.label: POFMA Directions remedy falsehood impact
sections.summary: In the case of POFMA, Directions are intended to remedy the impact of falsehoods, not those who deliberately create and spread them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: In the case of POFMA, Directions are intended to remedy the impact of falsehoods and not those who deliberately create and spread falsehoods.

sections.label: Adequacy of online falsehood tools
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Government can share how today's tools for dealing with online falsehoods are inadequate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: Can the Government share how the tools for dealing with online falsehoods today are inadequate?

sections.label: Communist disinformation and propaganda
sections.summary: Communist-supported disinformation and propaganda were widespread until the 1980s, and the Communist experience led to over 13,000 deaths over 12 years, ending in 1960.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Disinformation and propaganda of falsehoods supported by Communists in the region were widespread all the way until the 1980s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: This entire experience of the Communists led to over 13,000 deaths over 12 years, ending only in 1960.

sections.label: Jawi disinformation articles
sections.summary: Disinformation articles in Jawi manipulating the words of Singapore leaders were widespread, with an example from 17 July 1964.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Disinformation articles in Jawi manipulating the words of Singapore leaders were widespread, an example of which is this article from 17 July 1964.

sections.label: Bill gives clarification capability
sections.summary: The Bill gives the capability that was lacked then to put out clarifications and corrections fast, accurately and widely.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Today, this Bill gives us the capability we lacked then to put out clarifications, corrections fast, accurately and widely.

sections.label: Foreign state-linked disinformation evidence
sections.summary: The SC has received expert evidence of foreign state-linked disinformation already present in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: The SC has received expert evidence of foreign state-linked disinformation already present in Singapore.

sections.label: Herrmann describes weaponised narratives
sections.summary: Retired US Airforce Intelligence Colonel Jon Herrmann describes the V3S3 of weaponised narratives: vector, vulnerability and virulence; scope, speed and synergy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Retired US Airforce Intelligence Colonel Jon Herrmann describes what is known as the V3S3 of "weaponised narratives": vector, vulnerability and virulence; scope, speed and synergy.

sections.label: Virulence of fake news
sections.summary: Virulence today should be no surprise because fake news and falsehoods spread faster and wider than any given chemical weapons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Virulence today should be no surprise as well because fake news and falsehoods spread faster and wider than any given chemical weapons.

sections.label: Drip-feed falsehoods need swift action
sections.summary: The passage argues that drip-feed falsehoods by state-linked actors require swift action because their gradual effect can be hard to remedy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: But against this backdrop, the assertion that some drip-feed falsehoods should not require swift actions is misconceived.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: It is precisely drip-feed falsehoods that are the weapon of choice of state-linked actors today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Gradual insidious effect can take root deep in the population’s psyche.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Without a speedy reaction, it can be very difficult to remedy.

sections.label: Public decides, outside threats, Bill support
sections.summary: The speaker says the public decides right or wrong with both viewpoints, and supports the Bill due to outside threats needing robust measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: It is up to the public to decide, with the availability of both viewpoints, what is right or what is wrong.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: We are under threat from outside actors and that is something that requires robust measures to safeguard Singapore and Singaporeans, and that is why I support this Bill.

sections.label: Minister's power to remove election statements
sections.summary: The passage states the Bill gives a Minister absolute power to remove information that may influence an election, letting an incumbent party remove damaging statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The absolute power it bestows on a Minister to remove information that may influence the outcome of an election cannot be understated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: This Bill basically allows an incumbent party, who is seeking re‐election, the sole power to remove any damaging statement made against the party and its leaders, in the name of public interest, so as to contain any political fallout.

sections.label: Punggol East letter and Bill question
sections.summary: The passage describes a PAP letter about $22.5 million allegedly unaccounted for in Punggol East and asks how the Bill would deal with such a false statement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: At the eleventh hour of the campaign, the PAP machinery sent a letter to the residents of Punggol East, stating that $22.5 million belonging to the constituency and transferred to the accounts of the WP‐run Town Council in 2013 had become unaccounted for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The letter said it was an indisputable fact that the money had gone missing from our books, contrary to what was reported by our auditors every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Clearly, this false statement was made solely to influence the outcome of the 2015 elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: So, how would this proposed Bill, if it were to be in place, deal with this false statement of fact coming from the incumbent party at the very last minute, and regurgitated by the state media to reach a wider audience without any fact checking done?

sections.label: Minister discretion to take down statements
sections.summary: The passage says statements against an authority or its leadership that may be misconstrued can be taken down by a Minister's discretion without proving falsehood.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Any statement made against an entity of the authority or its leadership, which may not be outright false but could be misconstrued in the context in which it appears, can be taken down in the name of public interest under this Bill solely at the discretion of any Minister, without having first to prove the alleged falsehood.

sections.label: Minister abuse, courts, election timing
sections.summary: The passage questions what happens if a Minister abuses the Bill before hustings, noting courts may hear appeals in nine days and may not need to rule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: It is easy for the Law Minister to say, and I quote, "These Ministers are elected officials, and the decisions they make could also be reflected by the people's votes during a General Election." Sir, if an unscrupulous Minister were to abuse his power under this proposed Bill right before the hustings start, and win the election subsequently, what can the final arbiter of truth do?

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: And, as the Minister had said yesterday, the fastest time the Courts can hear an appeal in this instance is nine days, excluding weekends and public holidays.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: There are only nine days of campaigning, including weekends and public holidays.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: Under this Bill, the Courts may not even need to rule if the Minister were to subsequently agree with the aggrieved party, upon appeal, that the statement concerned was indeed not false.

sections.label: No confidence in future Government
sections.summary: The speaker says no one can vouch for how a future Government will act with this Bill, so he cannot support it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: The fact of the matter is: no one can vouch for how a future Government will act with this Bill, not just the Law Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
sentences.text: I cannot, with a clear conscience, support this Bill.

sections.label: Singaporeans using online news sources
sections.summary: Over 96% of Singaporeans under 50 get news online, as do 79% in their 50s and 63% in their 60s, up from five years ago.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: More than 96% of Singaporeans below the age of 50 regularly get their news from online sources.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Similarly, and perhaps more starkly, 79% of Singaporeans in their 50s and 63% of those in their 60s, use online news sources, compared to 35% and 10% just five years ago.

sections.label: Mobile data consumption doubling
sections.summary: IMDA reported that mobile data consumption in Singapore doubled between 2016 and 2018.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) reported that there has been a doubling of mobile data consumption in Singapore between 2016 and 2018.

sections.label: Cross-border data flows and digital trade
sections.summary: Singapore's cross-border data flows grew 65% yearly from 2012 to 2016, and its share of digitally-deliverable services trade nearly doubled from 3.5% to 6.5%.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: From 2012 to 2016, Singapore's cross-border data flows grew by 65% per annum to reach 24,000 gigabits per second, the highest per capita compared to other highly-digitalised economies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) Economic Survey of Singapore in the third quarter of 2017 reported that between 2005 and 2015, our share of global merchandise trade remained stable at about 2%, that is, the trade in goods.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: But our share of the global trade in digitally-deliverable services nearly doubled from 3.5% to 6.5%.

sections.label: Powers under the Bill
sections.summary: The Bill's powers range from Targeted Corrections to General Corrections and takedown Directions, exercisable only for false statements of fact in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The powers under the Bill range from Targeted Corrections, to General Corrections and, ultimately, Stop Communications or "takedown" Directions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: These powers, as have been emphasised several times, can be exercised only if, firstly, there is a false statement of fact and, secondly, it is in the public interest, as defined in the Bill, to act.

sections.label: Takedown notices under class licence scheme
sections.summary: Since the class licence scheme began in 1996, IMDA has issued only 39 takedown notices, averaging slightly more than one a year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Since the inception of the class licence scheme under the BA in 1996, IMDA has issued only 39 takedown notices.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: It is slightly more than one a year on average.

sections.label: Portfolio Ministers with judicial oversight
sections.summary: The speaker argues that vesting authority in Portfolio Ministers with judicial oversight best meets all three considerations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: And if each of these cases we expect one single authority to render a judgement in a timely manner and take expeditious action, I think that is a very tall order.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: I would argue that vesting the authority in Portfolio Ministers with the availability of judicial oversight, as proposed in the Bill, best meets all three considerations.

sections.label: Section 52 Alternative Authorities
sections.summary: The speaker says section 52 of the Act provides for Alternative Authorities during the Election period.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: I do not know whether he has read section 52 of the Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: That section provides clearly for Alternative Authorities during the Election period.

sections.label: New POFMA Office within IMDA
sections.summary: A new POFMA Office will be established within IMDA to be the Competent Authority.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Hence, to administer the Bill, we intend to establish a new POFMA Office – it may not be the most literary elegance – but it is calling a spade a spade.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: So, we will establish a new POFMA office within IMDA which will be the Competent Authority.

sections.label: Clause 48 Codes of Practice
sections.summary: Clause 48 of the Bill empowers the Competent Authority to issue one or more Codes of Practice.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: To that end, clause 48 of the Bill empowers the Competent Authority to issue one or more Codes of Practice.

sections.label: Intermediaries political advertisements and deprioritising falsehoods
sections.summary: Intermediaries must ensure political advertisements disclose their source, and the practice requires deprioritising online falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Intermediaries will have to ensure that political advertisements disclose who the source is.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Third, the practice will also require deprioritising online falsehoods.

sections.label: Feedback, Codes and Annexes
sections.summary: Feedback was incorporated into the Bill, and the Competent Authority will work with tech companies and intermediaries on Codes and Annexes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: We have sought to incorporate their feedback into the main body of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: We are working with the tech companies in developing the Codes of Practice, and the Competent Authority will also work with the intermediaries to develop company-specific Annexes to the Codes.

sections.label: Review of Codes of Practice
sections.summary: The Competent Authority will regularly review the Codes of Practice and Annexes to keep pace with technology, market and user changes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: The Competent Authority will regularly review these Codes of Practice and Annexes to ensure that they keep pace with developments in technology, market environment and user behaviour and preferences.

sections.label: Rejecting company content filtering
sections.summary: Ms Irene Quay asked about legislative routes tasking companies to monitor and filter content, which the speaker says is neither necessary nor desirable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Ms Irene Quay asked if we could consider legislative routes taken by other countries, where companies are tasked to proactively monitor and filter content.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: I would say in response that this is neither necessary nor desirable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: We do not want to outsource the responsibility for our national and public interest to private companies.

sections.label: Ministers assume responsibility
sections.summary: The approach is for Ministers to assume the responsibility.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: In contrast, our approach is for the Ministers to assume the responsibility.

sections.label: New tools against online falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill provides calibrated measures, with Portfolio Ministers issuing directives under judicial oversight, balancing swift action, accountability and expertise.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: First, it is abundantly clear that we need a new and fit-for-purpose set of regulatory tools to deal with the challenge of online falsehoods in the digital age.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: This legislation is a pragmatic response to that challenge, providing for a set of calibrated measures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: By vesting in Portfolio Ministers the authority to issue directives and providing for judicial oversight, the Bill strikes the best possible balance between the needs for swift action, accountability for decisions and the requisite domain expertise to make quick assessments.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: In drafting this legislation, we have engaged the tech companies and other stakeholders and sought to incorporate their concerns where possible.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: Ultimately, the scourge of online falsehoods is an ever-present and evolving threat.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
sentences.text: We need a concerted whole-of-nation effort, from citizens, industry, stakeholders and Government and, in particular, a well-informed and discerning citizenry is the first and most important line of defence against online falsehoods.

sections.label: False information about medicines
sections.summary: False information about statins and cancer treatments has led people to forgo medicines and lifesaving treatment.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: False information about statins, which are cholesterol-lowering medicines, has led to many people choosing not to go on these medicines and, so, significantly raising their risk of heart attacks.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Fake claims about cancer treatments have led many to forgo lifesaving treatment for curable tumours, in favour of treatments that have no known efficacy and which can even be dangerous.

sections.label: Fake medical news consequences
sections.summary: Fake medical news has contributed to measles epidemics and online falsehoods about the HPV vaccination programme.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: (In English): The consequences of fake medical news are clear to see.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: It is startling that we are now seeing measles epidemics around the world, with very real loss of life that could have been entirely preventable through vaccination, vaccination that increasing numbers are choosing to refuse partly due to untrue information available online.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Closer to home, the timely decision by the Ministry of Health to introduce anti-human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for female schoolchildren, which will save the lives of many of our future wives and mothers, has been greeted with the rise of online falsehoods regarding the vaccine, which seek to derail this very important and life-preserving programme.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Misleading information spread by the anti-vaccine movement using social media can cause parents to reconsider vaccinating their children, exposing them to significant health risks.

sections.label: Online falsehoods and domain Ministers
sections.summary: Speaker agrees domain Ministers should decide on falsehoods affecting their areas, citing public health urgency, and asks how corrective action is chosen.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: In fact, in a recent study by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, it showed that people are 70% more likely to share online falsehoods rather than facts.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Laws still need to be in place to safeguard the public interest and for public safety.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Hence, I agree that domain Ministers are best placed to decide if the falsehood concerning their area impacts public interest, as the correction of online medical falsehoods, for example, constitutes a public health urgency, and demands to be expedited, and speed here is indeed necessary.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Imminent or existing threats, either physical or in the online space, must be dealt with expediently, though I do agree that for the falsehoods, there should still be an appeals process, and the Courts should have the final say on what is false.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Here, I do seek a clarification from the Minister as to the process through which an online falsehood will be dealt with in terms of the action or the corrective action taken: how will it be decided if a simple corrective rebuttal is all that would be required, or if a takedown is needed?

sections.label: Law may be too narrow
sections.summary: The speaker says they hold a contrarian view that this law may in fact be a little bit too narrow.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: I am going to end by just making a little bit of a small comment.

sentences.speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: I actually have a contrarian view that perhaps this law may, in fact, be a little bit too narrow.

sections.label: Support for POFMA framework
sections.summary: The House agrees on tackling deliberate online falsehoods causing social and economic damage, differing only on the framework's form; the speaker supports POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: One thing, despite the sheer diversity of views, is clear.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: And that is that, all of us in this House agree that we need to assiduously tackle deliberate online falsehoods that have the potential to cause social and economic damage, by putting in place a response framework to prevent such hoaxes, misinformation and falsehoods from negatively impacting our society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Of course, where we differ is the form and manner of that framework.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I rise in support of POFMA as a mechanism that will curtail the potential dangers of falsehood and misinformation.

sections.label: Clarifying diminution of public confidence
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Government for clarity or examples of what counts as diminution of public confidence in public institutions or office bearers under POFMA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Could the Government please provide some clarity or examples of incidences on what it could consider as a diminution of public confidence in our public institutions or bearers of public office that would result in the Government exercising their powers under POFMA?

sections.label: Court appeals intimidating and costly
sections.summary: The speaker sees merits in Judiciary-handled appeals but says going to Court is intimidating, onerous and costly for individuals or organisations of modest means.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: So, I do see the merits of the appeals being handled by the Judiciary, which is set apart from the Executive Branch.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, Sir, the reality is that, for most people, the prospect of "going to Court" is an intimidating one and could actually be onerous and demanding, especially for individuals or organisations of modest means, who might not be financially equipped for such a legal appeals process, or who might just find the whole process of legal appeal via the Courts too overbearing and intimidating.

sections.label: Bill's benefits outweigh pitfalls
sections.summary: Despite concerns, the speaker believes the Bill's potential benefit far outweighs its potential pitfalls and concludes in support of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my concerns, I ultimately believe that the potential benefit of this Bill far outweighs the potential pitfalls, and I thus conclude my speech in support of the Bill.

sections.label: Appeal cost and duration
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister for details on how long further appeals to the Court of Appeal take and what they cost.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: First, in addition to the process of an appeal to the High Court, can the Minister also provide details of how long it would take and how much it might cost when cases go on further appeal to the Court of Appeal?

sections.label: Satire and comedy exclusion
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister to elaborate on how satire and comedy will be excluded from the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister elaborate on how satire and comedy will be excluded from the law?

sections.label: SC proposal on public information
sections.summary: The passage states the SC proposed public institutions pre-empt vulnerabilities and put out information in advance, and urges more resources and engagement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The SC itself proposed that public institutions should "pre-empt vulnerabilities and put out information in advance, where possible, to inoculate the public." The Government should channel more resources and take greater efforts to engage Singaporeans.

sections.label: Countries with information laws
sections.summary: The passage states that more than 80 countries have some form of freedom of information laws.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: More than 80 countries have some form of freedom of information laws.

sections.label: Government review update request
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister to share whether the Government is looking into this and to provide an update.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share whether the Government is looking into this and provide an update?

sections.label: Bill Parts 5 and 6 powers
sections.summary: The passage states Part 6 lets the Government direct an intermediary to stop an inauthentic account communicating and interacting in Singapore, and Part 5 covers repeatedly false websites.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Part 6 of the Bill empowers the Government to direct an intermediary to prevent an inauthentic account from communicating content within Singapore, and interacting with users in Singapore when the stipulated conditions are satisfied.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Part 5 of the Bill contains the levers relating to websites that put out falsehoods repeatedly.

sections.label: Directions and non-compliance offence
sections.summary: The Directions deal with the impact of falsehoods and are not punishments, but non-compliance without reasonable excuse is an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Directions deal with the impact of falsehoods; they are not punishments.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Non-compliance with the Direction, without reasonable excuse, is, however, an offence.

sections.label: Bill commencement date
sections.summary: The Bill will come into force on a date to be specified, with relevant subsidiary legislation, as is usual.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill will come into force hereafter, with relevant subsidiary legislation, on a date to be specified, as is usual.

sections.label: Word misleading and falsehoods
sections.summary: The word misleading reflects jurisprudence that statements can be false through omission, and the Bill deals with false material.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Some, including Mr Faisal Manap and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, have asked why do we use the word "misleading".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This reflects existing jurisprudence that statements can also be false by reason of having misled through omission.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: At the end of the day, whether by omission or by express statement, the Bill deals with material that is false.

sections.label: Satire and comedy excluded
sections.summary: By definition, once it talks about fact, satire and comedy are excluded, and the Act applies to falsehoods.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: By definition, once it talks about fact, then it excludes satire and comedy.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Say this is fact and falsehoods, the Act applies to falsehoods, then satire and parody is excluded.

sections.label: Public interest definitions
sections.summary: The Bill articulates the grounds of public interest with greater specificity and clarity than earlier laws.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You have seen the definitions of "public interest".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill actually articulates the grounds of public interest with greater specificity and clarity than in earlier laws.

sections.label: False claim about Sweden
sections.summary: A real example was a false claim that Swedish police had said there were 50 no go areas in Sweden.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The third example, a real example, was a false claim that Swedish police had said, "There were 50 'no go' areas in Sweden, filled with illegal immigrants, and these areas were too dangerous for even the police to enter".

sections.label: False claims sparking mob violence
sections.summary: False claims about Muslims and a Chinese woman led to armed mobs and unrest in Indonesia.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Within, I think 24 hours, armed mobs were on the streets because of a false claim that two Muslims had raped a Buddhist woman.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In Indonesia, there was a rumour that a Chinese woman threw items at a mosque and stopped prayers.

sections.label: Five hours wiped out billions
sections.summary: Within five hours, $4 billion was wiped out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Within five hours, it wiped out $4 billion.

sections.label: Three days of free hearing
sections.summary: The matter should be disposed of fairly quickly, but three days of free hearing are provided.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In fact, in my view, it should be disposed of fairly quickly, but we have provided for three days of free hearing.

sections.label: Reader decides, no criminal consequences
sections.summary: Readers can read both articles and decide, with no criminal consequences unless Directions are refused.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And then the reader is open to read this article, and he is open to read the other article and decide for himself.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, there are no criminal consequences, unless the person refuses to comply with the Directions.

sections.label: Narrower criminal provision for false statements
sections.summary: The criminal provision requires a false statement of fact and public interest impact, with no punishment if falsity is unknown.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I said yesterday, the criminal provision under the Bill is actually narrower because it requires both a false statement of fact and for public interest to be impacted.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you do not know that the content was false, then as I said yesterday, there is no question of criminal punishment.

sections.label: No academic carve-out for false statements
sections.summary: The Bill does not cover academic opinion but has no carve-out for academics making false statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill does not cover academic opinion but, in the same measure, as Minister Ong Ye Kung said, there is no carve-out for academics either, for statements which are false.

sections.label: Accurate facts and views
sections.summary: The speaker says accurate facts and views based on them are not within this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: All I can tell the Member is that I will make two general points: if the facts are accurate – meaning you set out whatever accurately – and the views are expressed based on those facts, it is not within this Bill.

sections.label: Freedom of Information Act effects
sections.summary: The passage quotes officials and Tony Blair saying freedom of information laws deter written candour in government.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But it basically means anyone can ask for any information, regardless of the reasons why and without having to be responsible as to how they will use it.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the key question for us in Parliament is when we put in a Freedom of Information Act, does it improve governance or does it affect governance?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: John Lloyd, Australia's Public Service Commissioner said, and I quote: "Ever since they introduced Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), public servants have a culture of 'don’t put it in writing'", because if you put it in writing, it can be FOIA-ed "due to the very pernicious Freedom of Information laws”.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: John Fraser, Australia’s Secretary of the Department of Treasury, said this: “Freedom of Information has made people extremely careful in the public service about what they put on paper and that is sad...Open policy debate means people have got to be candid.” So, it is affecting open debate within government because nobody wants to put it on paper because if you put it on paper, under the Freedom of Information Act somebody will get it.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Lord O’Donnell, former Cabinet Secretary and UK Head of Civil Service: "Civil servants were 'mentally' working on Brexit plans, to avoid the Freedom of Information Act." Tony Blair, 2010 – he introduced Freedom of Information Act – but after stepping down, he said in 2010: “The Freedom of Information Act…is a dangerous Act   governments need to be able to debate, discuss and decide issues in confidence." So, does it improve trust?

sections.label: Requesting information and responses
sections.summary: The passage states anyone can ask for information and will receive it or an explanation why not.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You can ask for any information that you want and we will either have to give you the information or we will have to explain to you why we cannot give it.

sections.label: POFMA as serious issue
sections.summary: The passage says POFMA addresses a serious issue and there is little disagreement that legislation is needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: POFMA is here to deal with a serious problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the question of whether there should be POFMA should be dealt with by reference to whether it is a serious issue that needs to be dealt with.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The SC says it is a serious issue.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have not heard any speech that says it is not a serious issue.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think there is very little disagreement that there should be legislation.

sections.label: Extent of government falsehoods
sections.summary: The passage asks about the extent of government falsehoods and damage to society from evidence laid out.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The second point I make is, what is the extent, what is the extent of the Government spreading falsehoods, and what has been the damage to society so far in the context of all the evidence that I have laid out to you, to the House, yesterday about how falsehoods have been damaging society after society, country after country around the world?

sections.label: Mislead Parliament means resign
sections.summary: The passage states that anyone who misleads Parliament must resign, with processes to haul them up.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
sentences.text: If you mislead Parliament, you will have to resign.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I am reminded by Senior Minister Teo that if you mislead Parliament, you will have to resign.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are serious processes available to haul up anyone who misleads Parliament – Member of Parliament or Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And certainly, on this side of the House, anyone who misleads Parliament will be made to resign.

sections.label: Bill powers narrower judicial oversight
sections.summary: The speaker sets out how the Bill's powers are narrower and there is more judicial oversight.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Two, I set out how the powers in the Bill are narrower and there is more judicial oversight.

sections.label: Chilling effect question to WP
sections.summary: The speaker asks how a narrower Bill with greater judicial oversight creates a greater chilling effect, a question WP Members side-stepped.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the Bill is narrower and there is greater judicial oversight, the crucial question that has been side-stepped by every single one of the WP Members of Parliament is: how does it then create a greater chilling effect?

sections.label: Bill narrower explained
sections.summary: The speaker says he has explained why the Bill is narrower.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Likewise, in this Bill, I have explained why the Bill is narrower.

sections.label: Mr Low POHA statement inaccurate
sections.summary: The speaker says Mr Low's statement that POHA's original purpose was only to protect individuals is inaccurate.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But there is one statement which Mr Low made which is inaccurate and seriously inaccurate.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He said on POHA, and I quote, "When POHA was passed in Parliament, the original purpose was only to protect individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But a few years ago, the Government then tried to include Government agencies as one of the groups protected by this Act." That is, on its face, not correct.

sections.label: POHA section 15 Government view
sections.summary: The Government believes section 15 of POHA applied to the Government, and accepted the Chief Justice's view.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But when it comes to statements, our view was that it can apply to the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, harassment, stalking, would be sections 3 to 7 of POHA as it existed, and section 15, the Government believes applied to the Government but not any of the other provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And the Government has never sought to rely on any of the other provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But on section 15, in the Court of Appeal, two Judges thought that it did not cover the Government, the Chief Justice thought that it did, and the Government accepted that view.

sections.label: Proposal requires going to Court
sections.summary: The speaker says the proposal would require people to go to Court in every case because the Government would sue them.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The point that both of you make is that people do not want to go to Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But what you are proposing will require people to go to Court in every single case because you want the Government to sue them.

sections.label: Lee Kuan Yew 1963 speech
sections.summary: The speaker cites Lee Kuan Yew's 1963 speech when Barisan opponents disrupted him while staying unseen.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They might be people working with foreign state actors.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it is more sensible, what we are proposing.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Something that Mr Lee Kuan Yew said a very long time ago.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He was making a speech in 1963 in the days when Barisan was active.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think the opponents were shouting, disrupting when he was speaking, but they did so while remaining in the dark.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They wanted to disrupt and engage in rowdyism but did not themselves want to be seen.

sections.label: Minister versus Court sequence
sections.summary: The Government and opposition agree legislation is needed but differ on whether Courts or Ministers decide first.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In essence, as I read the speeches, the main point of difference with the Government appears to be that we agree it is a problem, we agree it is serious, we agree legislation is necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In fact, I do not even think there is much disagreement on the provisions but in terms of sequence – let the Court decide first instead of the Minister, whereas the Government's position is Ministers decide, subject to an appeal which will be quick.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What the Government has proposed achieves the objective, subjects the Government to oversight, strikes the right balance and, in fact, is a narrowing of the powers from what they are today.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you apply the WP's proposal of the Courts first, you cannot be sure that you can act speedily.

sections.label: Court-first proposal complications
sections.summary: The respondent's proposal could become complicated and time-consuming even with a standby judge.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In your proposal, the respondent has no choice – can become a very complicated exercise, taking time, even if we resource the Courts in such a way that there is a judge on standby all the time.

sections.label: Bill narrower in powers
sections.summary: The speaker says opponents do not address that the Bill is narrower in powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: First of all, they do not deal with the point that the Bill is narrower in powers.

sections.label: Act first or Court first
sections.summary: The real issue is whether to act immediately against falsehoods then face Court, or go to Court first.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The real point is not the speeches about the importance of free speech – which no one can argue about – but whether we should act immediately to stop the flow of falsehoods and then be subject to the Court, or whether it should go to Court first.

sections.label: Election powers by civil servants
sections.summary: Minister Iswaran pointed out that during elections civil servants, not Ministers, exercise the powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: My colleague Minister Iswaran has pointed out that, during elections, the powers are exercised by civil servants, not Ministers.

sections.label: AOJPA codified existing law
sections.summary: AOJPA largely codified existing law, made necessary procedural changes and classified how offences were to be investigated.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: AOJPA largely codified existing law, introduced procedural changes which were necessary and classified how offences were to be investigated.

sections.label: MPs' quotes on AOJP fears
sections.summary: The speaker quotes Pritam Singh, Dennis Tan and Leon Perera on fears the Bill creates, and asks whether that came to pass.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Pritam Singh, I quote: "Viewed in totality, the Government's approach gives it significant powers to strike fear in the heart of ordinary citizens." Mr Dennis Tan, I quote: "This Bill, if passed, creates a huge shadow of fear hanging over Singaporeans who may otherwise have justified opinions on certain topical issues." Has that come to pass, Mr Tan?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you go out there and talk to the man-in-the-street and tell him AOJP, what do you think the answer will be?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Leon Perera, not to be outdone, "The result for our democracy from the passage of this Bill and the attendant publicity could well be that no one who does not have $100,000 in cash to spare will dare to speak up about any issue where there is even the slightest risk or perceived risk of prosecution under this law." Earlier, I referred to Mr Low Thia Khiang and his references to the ISA when speaking on the AOJP as well.

sections.label: Balancing urgency and decision-maker
sections.summary: The key issue was balancing the urgency of acting against an online falsehood with having a more acceptable decision-maker than an unchecked Executive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The key issue for us was, as I said in my speech, to balance the urgency of moving against an online falsehood and having a decision-maker that is more acceptable than an unchecked Executive.

sections.label: Goh Yihan's SC submission
sections.summary: The speaker cites Prof Goh Yihan's submission to the SC, paragraph 27, as a matter of Parliamentary record.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: If we look at Prof Goh Yihan's submission to the SC – and this is public information, it is a matter of Parliamentary record – paragraph 27: "I set out below a summary of the discussion above...," he goes.

sections.label: ISA versus POFMA powers
sections.summary: The passage contrasts the ISA, which does not deal with the falsehood itself, with POFMA's scoped and sharpened powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: ISA – covers only falsehoods likely to cause public alarm, does it deal with the falsehood itself? – "No." But under POFMA, these matters are actually resolved because the powers are scoped.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: We can, again, like I said, reasonable people can have different views about which words to use, but one can also argue that under POFMA, the Government's powers are actually sharpened.

sections.label: Countries with FOI regimes
sections.summary: About 110 countries have some FOI regime, and about 80 introduced such legislation in the last 30 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: If we look at FOI from memory, I think there are about 110 countries in the world that have some sort of FOI regime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But out of these 110 countries, about 80 of them only introduced an FOI or FOI-like legislation over the last 30 years.

sections.label: POFMA not a silver bullet
sections.summary: The passage states that POFMA is not a silver bullet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: In the same way, POFMA is not a silver bullet.

sections.label: Examples and uncovered issues
sections.summary: The Minister raised examples about Ferrero Roche and toilet paper, but some requests uncovered issues like the UK expenses scandal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
