sentences.text: The Minister raised some examples about Ferrero Roche, consumption of Ferrero Roche Rock chocolates, toilet paper.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But we also have to remember that some of these requests actually uncovered issues like the expenses scandal, the Member of Parliament's expenses' scandal in the UK.

sections.label: Sharpened Bill and existing legislation
sections.summary: The speaker says everything wanted under the Bill can be done under existing legislation, save for territoriality.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You said it is "sharpened", I explained why everything that we want to do under the Bill can be done under existing legislation and subsidiary legislation, save for the point on territoriality.

sections.label: Minister decides falsehood and correction
sections.summary: The Minister decides whether a statement is falsehood, interprets if it is fact or opinion, and decides to take it down or issue a correction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: First of all, the Minister makes that decision on whether it is falsehood and he interprets any statement whether it is a statement of fact or whether it is opinion, and he makes a decision to say, "Okay, let's take it down" or "Put out a statement of correction." The decision is made.

sections.label: ISA Minister decides security
sections.summary: In ISA, a Minister decides what is security and national interest, and says a person should be locked up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: In ISA, the Executive, a Minister, basically decides what is security, what is national interest, and then, say, "Okay, you should be locked up.

sections.label: POFMA deals with freedom of expression
sections.summary: POFMA deals with freedom of expression because people say something and you decide whether it is correct or factual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: The important thing is, POFMA deals with freedom of expression because people say something, and you decide whether this is correct, whether it is factual.

sections.label: Ministerial powers against tech companies
sections.summary: A speaker says opinions are not covered by the Bill but expects Ministers using its powers to be careful, as it may be used against tech companies and platforms.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Your opinions could be wrong, your opinions could be false, but that is not covered by the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But I have no doubt that any Minister who wants to exercise his powers under the Bill when it becomes an Act and if Parliament agrees, will have to be very careful, because, while I have not gone into it in great detail, it is primarily something that might be used against tech companies and platforms.

sections.label: Hansard and POHA court ruling
sections.summary: A speaker asks the Minister to confirm the Court of Appeal examined Second Reading Hansard and found the Government not a proper applicant, and asks about proportionality and appeals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The circumstances, if I remembered it, were that the Government tried to apply under POHA against a falsehood rather than for harassment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I wonder if the Minister could confirm that actually what the Court of Appeal said in its decision was that it examined what was said during the Second Reading of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: And looking at what was recorded in the Hansard, the Minister, in fact, had only referred to scenarios involving vulnerable victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, the Court of Appeal came to the conclusion that looking at the intention that was expressed during the Second Reading in the Hansard, the Government was not a proper person to apply because that was not the intention that was articulated in Parliament, which, of course, raises concerns about the effect of Hansard today for future actions of the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I believe he did say something like this.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, I would like him to clarify that because looking at the grounds of appeal, it does not look as if the High Court can look into proportionality.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Proportionality relates to the kind of remedies that might be directed like takedowns or corrections, and it would be judicial review.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Appeal is just on a question of fact or falsehood.

sections.label: Part 4 directives and accountability
sections.summary: A speaker argues Part 4 directives stopping embarrassing information may chill free expression, cowed investigative journalism and lack of public interest defence may insulate Ministers from electoral accountability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I think it has been said that the Ministers make decisions, Part 3, Part 4 directives, they will be held to account by the electorate, they are accountable to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I did make the argument that, actually, by using a Part 4 directive to stop the circulation of potentially embarrassing information, the presence of a chilling effect on free expression – which I think we have talked about – the possibility that efforts at investigative journalism will be cowed due to the lack of a public interest defence within the Bill, as a result of that, potentially embarrassing information may not come into circulation and that may, in fact, partly insulate the Minister from electoral accountability and may even affect the composition of the Parliament that is meant to hold the Minister accountable.

sections.label: Recourse for fake news victims
sections.summary: A speaker asks what recourse a victim of such Government fake news would have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: What recourse would a victim of such Government fake news have?

sections.label: POFMA widening falsehood definition
sections.summary: A speaker reads clause 45 of the TA and says POFMA widens the definition by deeming misleading statements false and covering reason to believe something is false.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Clause 45 of the TA, very briefly, let me read it: "Any person who transmits or causes to be transmitted a message which he knows to be false or fabricated shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction", and so on and so on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Now, there are two senses in which actually the definition of that is widened in POFMA because POFMA allows for a misleading statement to be deemed false, meaning a collection of true statements that are misleading could be deemed false.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Also, POFMA says that if you have reason to believe that something is false.

sections.label: POFMA criminal penalties versus TA
sections.summary: A speaker says POFMA's section 7 criminal penalties against individuals appear to widen powers and penalties compared with the TA and BA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: In this regard, vis-a-vis the criminal penalties against individuals, which is in section 7 of POFMA, POFMA will appear to widen powers and penalties, insofar as that is concerned vis-a-vis TA and BA.

sections.label: Bill falsehood and public interest
sections.summary: The Bill's primary factors are that the statement must be false and of public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The primary factors, as far as the Bill is concerned is, it has got to be false, and it has got to be of public interest.

sections.label: Lowered test and court risk
sections.summary: The test was deliberately made lower, an appeal rather than judicial review, with courts able to embarrass them.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But I keep emphasising that there is a sword hanging over with the Courts, and if we get it wrong, we will be publicly embarrassed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And we have deliberately made the test lower as in, it is an appeal rather than a judicial review.

sections.label: Two mens rea requirements
sections.summary: The Bill requires proving intention for both misleading falsehood and public interest, unlike the TA's single requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You have two things to prove in terms of intention, not just the misleading falsehood part, but also public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the TA, the knowledge of harm to public interest is not necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, there are two mens rea requirements under the Bill, as opposed to one mens rea requirement under the TA.

sections.label: Future subsidiary legislation delay risk
sections.summary: A future Minister or Government could change subsidiary legislation to delay appeals and obstruct swift judicial oversight.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Again, we welcome the Minister outlining the details of the subsidiary legislation that addresses these amendments in this regard yesterday.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: However, any future Minister and/or Government could still make changes in the subsidiary legislation to enact rules to unnecessarily delay the appeal process, obstructing appellants' access to swift judicial oversight.

sections.label: Independent Council against online falsehoods
sections.summary: A New Clause is introduced for an Independent Council to evaluate actions, make recommendations and report annually.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Mr Chairman, I beg to introduce a New Clause entitled "Independent Council to strengthen society against online falsehoods".

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move that the New Clause* be read a Second time.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
sentences.text: The Council will be empowered to routinely evaluate the actions taken under this Act, make recommendations to the Government and provide accountability to the public through annual reports on the Act.
